messages.subject: Re: Asking about the NBLAST
parts:
Dear Xufei Du,

Many thanks for your interest in the NBLAST method. This is a good
question that several people have asked in the past and one that we have
asked ourselves when we worked with the zebrafish mitral cell data used
in the 2016 NBLAST paper. Our approach was quite simple – just to
scale the zebrafish data until the physical size of the brain matched
the fly brain. This actually works surprising well in our hands – in
fact the size of fish and fly brains is not as different as you might
imagine and scale factors in the range 1 (i.e. no scaling) to 1/2 (i.e.
reduce size by fact of 2x) gave reasonable results. Essentially what you
want is for the curvature of neuronal structures and the reproducibility
of position in space (SD +/- 2.5µm per axis in flies) to match.

There is no doubt that a better approach would be to calculate a new
scoring matrix based on data transformed to a fish template brain.
However to prepare this you would need to have many pairs of true
positive matches in your dataset. Those 150 PNs contained a rather
smaller number of types, so my recollection is that we were able to make
> 1000 combinations.

Finally you can also use the NBLAST v1 implementation. This is a simpler
implementation without a score matrix but where you specify sigma, a
user selected spatial distance parameter. For example this was recently
used in a new mouse study from the Allen Institute:

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.02.03.932244v1.full


Best,

Greg.

PS I have taken the liberty of ccing this message to the nat-user google
group since the answer may be of interest to others.

--

On 12 Mar 2020, at 4:53, 杜旭飞 wrote:

> Dear Prof. Jefferis,
>
> Sorry to disturb you. I am Xufei Du, a senior engineer at the
> Institute of Neuroscience, Chinese Academy of Sciences, in
> Shanghai. Recently, our lab got many single neuron reconstructions in
> larval zebrafish and wanted to classify them by using your efficient
> and beautiful algorithm NBLAST. I wrote to ask one point concerning
> the pairwise similarity score.
>
> In your work, you got the scoring matrix based on Drosophila’s data
> (150 PNs and 5000 random pairs), so I’m wondering, based on your
> experience and thinking, when I apply the NBLAST to another species,
> is it necessary to generate the specific scoring matrix for that
> animal and even for different developmental stages. And will the
> scoring matrix be influenced by the pair number chosen for the same
> and random groups?
>
> I’m looking forward to your reply and thanks for your time.
>
> Sincerely yours,
>
> Xufei Du

messages.author: 7f0257cd1389289f
messages.subject: Re: Asking about the NBLAST
parts:
Dear Xufei,

Thanks for the additional query. This is also a question that has come
up regularly e.g.

https://groups.google.com/forum/m/#!searchin/nat-user/soma/nat-user/x1ysfWRm4TI

I have at least two strategies to improve things, but nothing ready yet.
The easiest one mentioned in that thread you could do fairly easily
yourself by taking out the soma and computing a distance score on that.
However you might look at the position with respect to the brain surface
or neuropil. And the spatial precision might be different from neurites.

Best,

Greg.
